title: Prior-based Noisy Text Data Filtering: Fast and Strong Alternative For Perplexity
claim: Token priors are highly skewed: frequent function words sit on top, content words in the middle, and noisy tokens at the bottom.
layout: Central line plot with shaded zones; three token tables linked by dashed arrows
description: A central line plot shows log token prior (y-axis, about -5 to -37) against token rank (x-axis, 0 to 50000). The black curve drops steeply at the start, flattens through a long middle section, then plunges at the end. The background is shaded in three bands: lavender for the high-prior head, green for the middle, and pink for the low-prior tail. Red dashed circles mark one point in each region. Dotted gray arrows link the circles to three grid tables of example tokens. The left table, titled 'High prior zone (function words)', lists tokens such as 'the', 'and' and 'of'. The upper-right table, 'Middle prior zone (content words)', lists words such as 'colder' and 'Creation'. The lower-right table, 'Low prior zone (noise)', lists garbled strings and spam fragments. The eye goes first to the curve, then to the tables.
caption: The line graph shows the logarithm of token priors (based on the GPT-2 tokenizer) computed from the Dolma dataset, sorted in descending order. The boxed regions highlight tokens from the top, middle, and bottom segments of the rank.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are pretrained on massive web corpora, careful selection of data becomes essential to ensure effective and efficient learning. While perplexity (PPL)-based filtering has shown strong performance, it suffers from drawbacks: substantial time costs and inherent unreliability of the model when handling noisy or out-of-distribution samples. In this work, we propose a simple yet powerful alternative: a prior-based data filtering method that estimates token priors using corpus-level term frequency statistics, inspired by linguistic insights on word roles and lexical density. Our approach filters documents based on the mean and standard deviation of token priors, serving as a fast proxy to PPL while requiring no model inference. Despite its simplicity, the prior-based filter achieves the highest average performance across 20 downstream benchmarks, while reducing time cost by over 1000x compared to PPL-based filtering. We further demonstrate its applicability to symbolic languages such as code and math, and its dynamic adaptability to multilingual corpora without supervision
